Help a brother out with a diet?

Bodybuilding.com is a good resource. They have calculators and decent articles.

Essentially, as Legionality says, you need to determine your macros. Macros are protein, carbs, fats. I try to target a 40%/30%/30% split. A friend of mine does 50%/30%/20%. Partly it's determined by what type of exercise regime you are doing. Protein should be 1-1.5 grams per lb of body weight, for the weight you are targeting.

Most importantly, starting out you need to be weighing your food and writing down all your macros for every meal until you get the idea of how much food you eat. This is the most important thing to learning what kind of diet you are practicing.
Protip: try Wolfram Alpha search engine for calorie counting, their calculator is fantastic. For example 150g brown rice + 200g chicken.
What exactly are you trying to do? Are you trying to lose weight, build muscle, get stronger, or all three?

I apologize for the wall of text, but I think it's worth it to read it! Just to show I know what I'm talking about, here is a 4 month progress pic that was only possible for me through a very strict diet: Before: http://i.imgur.com/a9Eckyp.jpg After: http://i.imgur.com/L7LtlVf.jpg

First you need to have a goal in mind before tailoring your diet. Do you want to lose or gain weight? Do you want to maintain your weight but get stronger (note this is slower than the two alternatives)? Once you have your goal in mind, you should calculate your TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expidenture). There are plenty of calculators online. Try a few of them and take the average to give you an idea of what your TDEE is. Once you know that, you should either eat your TDEE plus or minus 500 cals/day for gaining or losing weight respectively. MyFitnessPal is very useful for tracking calories. If you want to be very exact, buy a food scale and measure everything you can.

As far as what specific foods you should eat, you want to get around 1g/lb bodyweight of protein a day. Lean meats are great for hitting this goal. I eat chicken breasts and fish very regularly. Other good protein foods are cottage cheese, plain greek yogurt, whey protein, eggs, cheese, and milk. There are plenty of others, but those are some of my favorites to make sure I hit my protein goals. If your goal is to gain weight (muscle) then you can eat fatty meats too to get your protein.

Vegetables are the shit. Seriously, they provide satiety, have very little calories, and are packed with nutrients. I regularly eat a spinach/kale/chard mix I really like from Sam's club. Broccoli, mushrooms, onions, peppers, cucumbers, celery, potatoes, and carrots are some of my favorites. These will all help you feel full on a lower calorie diet, making losing weight much easier. Eating a couple servings of vegetables a day goes a long way in making sure you're not missing out on essential nutrients and keeping you full. Fruits are also good for providing nutrients and fullness, but they tend to have more calories than vegetables, so I try not to eat them too much when I'm working on losing weight.

You should try to stay away from processed foods unless your goal is to gain weight. They are very dense in calories and not nearly as filling as natural ingredients.

Also, you mentioned you stay away from GMOs in your post. There is actually no scientific evidence that GMOs are bad for you, so there is no need to avoid them!

Are idle games easy to code?
What do you mean by "idle games"? Turn based? Casual games?

idle games are a growing genre of games where, some degree of progress is made without player intervention. A game where you gain 1 dollar per second, with the only requirement be that the game is open, you then use this currency to buy upgrades, which have an effect on how much money you earn per second....

this is a very simplified example, good idle games (IMO) generally have multiple systems of customization and more then just one currency.
Kongregrate has a whole section for idle games.

Yeah. Well, I've only poked around in it a bit. If you know how to write functional JavaScript it's easy. The hard part is balance and coming up with a fun formula. From my limited experience with them, I know you need:

  • The click function
    This is the first and only available action the player can take, initially (in most cases). Click to collect some kind of resource. Write a function like this:

    var points = 0; // Track total points here
var bonus = 0; // If you use modifiers for higher points per click, use this
var theClick = function(n) {
 if ( n > 1 ) {
 points = points + ( n * (1 + bonus));
 } else {
 points = points + (1 + bonus);
 }
}

    Then just apply that function to a button in your interface. The n argument is explained below in the repeated function.

  • Resource(s)
    In my example above, points are your primary resource. You'll earn it from your theClick() function. You can get creative and come up with multiple resources (with multiple functions) to add more depth to your game. This is good if you want to add a rarer resource later in the game.

  • The repeating function
    Next you need to write a function that repeats every X seconds. This is used if you have "clickers" in your game. Any kind of upgrade that does the clicking for you. In the above example, I've included an argument to your function. Use this argument with the number of clickers the player currently has. Example: 

     var clickers = 3;
 setInterval(
 theClick(clickers), 1000;
 )

    This will fire your function every 1000ms (1 second). It passes the number of clickers as the argument, which multiplies the effect of the function. In the above example, it will add 3 to your points every 1 second.

  • Upgrades
    Upgrades add depth and interest to your game. This could be something like a percentage bonus to clicks, or doubling the effectiveness of your clickers.

Those are the core building blocks of any idle clicker game. The funnest games have many more layers to them, adding hundreds of upgrades, new resource types, animations, etc. It's a good exercise for someone who is an intermediate at JavaScript coding to build one of these kinds of games.

I was wondering, how do you handle really big values (like billions of billions) ? Do you cut your value into several int (i.e. var value1 = 999, var value 2 = 0, when value1>999; value2 ++ )?

I haven't really spent much time dealing with large numbers in my projects. The typical way I've seen is go up to 999 then convert to 1.00K, then 1.00M, 1.00B, 1.00T, 1.00Qa, 1.00Qi, 1.00Sx, 1.00Sp, 1.00O, 1.00N, and so on. That way the most digits you display would be five (999.99K). You can use a simple if statement to determine if the value should be displayed as K, M, etc. The back end value would remain the same. 980520001 would simply display as 980.52M for instance.
